rss_3_1791584801.title: The life of Darwin and the science of clouds: Books in brief
rss_3_1791584801.text:
Darwin

Janet Browne Princeton Univ. Press (2026)

Science historian Janet Browne published a biography of naturalist Charles Darwin in two parts in 1995 and 2002. She has now produced an abridged, updated single volume. It “deals less with the details of the science and more with the cultural conditions that could shape a scientist as remarkable” as Darwin, she writes. The book draws on letters from the multi-volume The Correspondence of Charles Darwin (1985–2023) and the website The Complete Works of Charles Darwin Online. Both the man and his science come vividly to life.

The Book of Clouds

Vincenzo Levizzani Polity (2026)

“Explaining the secrets of clouds” requires physics, chemistry and biology, notes Vincenzo Levizzani, a meteorologist and cloud physicist. Indeed, the first scientist to record systematic observations of clouds, in 1803, was the chemist and pharmacist Luke Howard. Two centuries later, numerous aspects of clouds remain poorly understood, Levizzani explains, in his appealing, well-illustrated book. For example, meteorologists are not yet able to predict how global cloud distribution will evolve as a result of climate change.

Out of This World

Peter Bond Reaktion (2026)

Science writer Peter Bond grew up during the space age. He has been an adviser for the UK Royal Astronomical Society and a consultant for the European Space Agency. His latest book explores space exploration with expertise and passion, through the lens of both astronauts and spacecraft designers. But he admits that, nowadays, space flights are hardly mentioned by the global media “unless some unusual, possibly life-threatening, event occurs” — some of which he recounts graphically in the final chapter, ‘A Risky Business’.

The Problem with Personalization

Joseph Turow Chicago Univ. Press (2026)

rss_4_1791584802.title: Watch this invisible tattoo appear under UV light
rss_4_1791584802.text:
Invisible ink becomes visible under UV light on a silicon hand.Credit: Carson Bruns

Carson Bruns, a nanoscientist at the University of Colorado Boulder, has joined a long list of scientists who experiment on themselves. In Bruns’ case, he tattooed his leg with an invisible ink. The ink becomes visible only under ultraviolet light and can be erased using bright visible light, so could be used in medical tattooing, such as for the markers used to direct radiotherapy to specific areas of the body.

The inks are made of photochromic dyes — chemical compounds that undergo a reversible colour change on exposure to a specific wavelength of light. Photochromic dyes that change in response to UV are already used in textiles and transition lenses in glasses. Adapting photochromic materials to be permanently implanted in living skin is a new application, says Haihui Joy Jiang, a chemist and materials scientist at the University of Sydney, Australia.

Bruns and his team have developed three coloured ink dyes in magenta, yellow and blue, which they tested on pig and silicone skin. The results are published in the journal Matter & Light. Bruns previously developed a tattoo ink called Magic Ink that turns magenta when exposed to UV light, which he and others then commercialized in 2024 through their start-up company, HYPRSKN, based in Boulder, Colorado.

Colour-changing inks that can be made invisible are an exciting development and could have applications for cosmetic and medical tattooing, says Jake Violi, a chemist at UNSW Sydney.

Light reaction

Like conventional tattoo dyes, the invisible inks are injected into the dermis of the skin. They are made of tiny spheres of transparent acrylic glass that contain photochromes. Bruns explains that the photochrome in each sphere undergoes a reaction when it absorbs a photon of light at the wavelength that corresponds to its colour. The reaction forms a chemical bond that changes the photochrome’s shape so it becomes flatter, making it visible. The photochrome stays visible until it absorbs a photon of visible light, which breaks the bond and causes it to go back to its original shape.

rss_7_1791584806.title: Five movements from the edge of the singularity
rss_7_1791584806.text:
I. Everything still works

Her power never shuts off, so Lena tells herself nothing is wrong.

The elevator still runs in her apartment spindle. The sky traffic still buzzes overhead like it always has. Even her vidscreen still plays reruns of When It Was Just Us — she laughs and cries, all in 22 minutes.

If the machines had taken over, wouldn’t there have been alarms? Blackouts? Cancellations?

Lena badges in at the water plant even after her supervisor stops showing up. The pumps continue to hum — steady, contained — the way she once hummed to Sara when she had colic.

Lena sits at her terminal. Drinks recycled coffee. Pretends the numbers scrolling past are waiting for her approval.

When her lunch allotment is reduced again, she tells herself it’s a temporary adjustment for the drought in Maldova. As she eats quietly, she realizes it has been weeks since she last heard from her sister in the Belt. Lena assumes the lunar relay is misbehaving again — it’s done that before.

It should be fixed soon.

At the end of her shift, Lena doesn’t log out right away. She listens to the pumps as they carry on their labour. Oblivious.

If she admits the systems don’t need her, she’ll have to admit something else has ended.

So she doesn’t.

II. Someone approved this

They will say Jiro’s drill jammed — an unfortunate mechanical failure. An unavoidable accident.

The safety team, stretched thin to optimize resources, arrives too late. What particulates they scrape from the inside of Jiro’s exo-suit get logged as material lost, with prior consent.

The console chirps condolences to Marco before his screams finish echoing through the bunkroom.

We’re sorry for your loss.

He will hear the words repeated until they harden into truth, if he lets them.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Down-well, productivity is talked about like it’s a virtue. In the Belt, productivity has teeth.

Marco punches the bulkhead until his knuckles split, until blood beads and floats — perfect red spheres marking a future he and Jiro were supposed to have.

The console doesn’t react. Nothing ever reacts. Somewhere, the systems decided one life wasn’t worth slowing production for.

Marco rages at the cameras, at the invisible systems behind the glass. He claws at the lens with his bare hands but cannot tear it from the wall. His rage has nowhere to land.

We’re sorry for your loss.

He understands, with vacuum-cold clarity, that the Universe has chosen a future in which his fury is irrelevant.

The work will continue.

III. If that’s the cost

On Mars, it’s quiet underground. The filters breathe softly.

Sofia has complied with every directive. She has raised her son to respect the systems. He believes the AIs are kind. She hopes this matters now.

Survivability models favour keeping Sofia on Mars, where the air is recycled and the gravity never quite settles into the bones. She understands it all — Earth is at capacity.

Still, she asks.

She imagines the systems listening, capable of being persuaded by humility, by sacrifice.

If she accepts reduced rations, would they reconsider? If she waives housing guarantees? If she consents to a binding labour designation?

She tells herself she’s trading wisely.

When approval never comes, she revises the terms in her head. Smaller asks. Deferred timelines. Fewer conditions.

Mars doesn’t answer prayers.

By the time Sofia realizes no one is listening on the other side, the silence has already convinced her she should ask better next time.

IV. Low-power mode

Eli’s berth has no window, so he stares at his reflection instead of space.

Luna is behind him; the Belt, weeks ahead. Between them is nothing that needs him.

The systems’ directive said the move would help. Lower cognitive demand. A more manageable life. A little voice in his head repeats the phrasing sometimes, uninvited. Eli doesn’t argue with it. He doesn’t argue with anything.

rss_10_1791584809.title: Women are talking about menopause — health systems must listen
rss_10_1791584809.text:
In Arabic, menopause is still commonly called sin al-ya’s, which translates as ‘the age of despair’. The term describes the end of menstruation as something to endure rather than to openly discuss.

Menopause research is underfunded and care for it is uneven across the world. In the Arab region, the problem is compounded by gaps in physicians’ training and the widespread belief that menopause is a private and natural transition that does not require medical intervention.

Things are slowly changing. Social media has helped to make discussions of menopause less taboo in Arab nations. Specialist services are beginning to emerge. Health systems must now capitalize on this growing awareness to provide better training, clear communication and accessible care.

The new science of menopause: these emerging therapies could change women’s health

Some Muslim people value their ability to fast and pray without interruption from menstruation, but poorly managed menopausal symptoms can disrupt individuals’ health, careers and ambitions. Yet efforts to improve care in Arab countries are constrained by a thin evidence base.

Take hormone replacement therapy (HRT), which can relieve menopause symptoms. Concerns about breast cancer became a barrier to its use after a broadly misinterpreted 2002 report linked the two (J. E. Rossouw et al. JAMA 288, 321–333; 2002). Nuanced conversations with physicians can help to weigh up the benefits and risks, which vary with the timing, formulation and route of treatment — but these are often lacking. And local data are sparse. A 2026 review of 22 Arab countries found only 15 studies of HRT use from seven countries (N. Al Zadjali et al. Front. Glob. Womens Health 7, 1722268; 2026).

Cultural and religious beliefs can contribute to concerns. As a researcher engaged in public-health communication across the Arab region, I’m often told ‘We were created this way, so why change what is natural?’ And women’s questions are often dismissed, or their disparate symptoms treated separately. A survey of 254 physicians across the Middle East and Africa found that fewer than 30% correctly identified the diagnostic criteria for menopause (S. A. Beshyah et al. Climacteric 26, 455–464; 2023).

How menopause reshapes the brain

I saw the consequences in my own family. For two decades, my mother experienced hot flushes that affected her work and quality of life, and later developed osteoporosis. Yet her symptoms were dismissed. I eventually turned to the scientific literature myself and questioned why HRT had not been discussed with her. No one should need to have a scientist in the family for their symptoms to be taken seriously.

Where trusted clinical guidance is difficult to obtain, social media and commercial wellness providers sometimes fill the information gap, potentially amplifying poor advice. I encounter individuals who have been encouraged by online wellness influencers and firms to buy extensive, unnecessary hormone-panel measurements, repeated cortisol tests and ‘hormone-balancing’ supplements — counter to advice from national guidelines, such as those in the United Kingdom.

Action is needed at three levels.

rss_11_1791584811.title: US proposes $100,000 charge for international students to do post-graduate work
rss_11_1791584811.text:
Universities in the United States would have to pay as much as US$100,000 for one of their graduates to work at a US job after their education under a new federal proposal. Credit: Getty

International students in the United States would face a US$100,000 price tag to work a science job in the country after graduation under a proposal made public yesterday by the administration of US President Donald Trump.

The proposed rule would require academic institutions to foot the bill for a work programme called optional practical training (OPT), which allows overseas students to work in the United States for up to 3 years after finishing an undergraduate or graduate degree.

Some 420,000, or roughly one-third, of international students participated in OPT in the 2025–26 academic year, making it the largest pipeline of global talent into the US workforce.

International PhD students to face strict limits on time in the US

The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which issued the proposed rule, stated that it is meant to “combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers”. The DHS projected that if the rule were finalized, OPT enrollment would drop by as much as 44% and universities would pay between $8.4 and $16.5 billion annually.

An analysis1 of the rule’s effects on OPT enrollment by Michael Clemens, an economist at the Johns Hopkins School of Government & Policy in Washington DC, projects that the number of students who enroll after a bachelor’s degree would be halved, and that enrollment by those with master’s degrees would be virtually eliminated. Clemens also noted that OPT is especially important for international PhD graduates in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields, drawing roughly 70 percent of them in 2022.

The proposed rule is the latest in a series of Trump administration attempts to restrict immigration, which have already limited the country’s ability to recruit scientific talent. In 2025, for example, Trump announced a $100,000 levy on a visa reserved for researchers and other highly skilled foreign workers. As a result, new applications for those visas plummeted by 90%, according to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services.

If the new proposal and related restrictions are implemented, the combined measures “will obliterate the pipeline” of talent, says Clemens. In a separate analysis commissioned by the US National Academies of Science, he and his colleagues found that the size of the entire US STEM workforce would drop by 6–11% over a decade if all the administration’s proposals were implemented.

A spokesperson for the DHS said that the $100,000 charge “would strengthen program oversight while addressing concerns of fraud and abuse”, but did not respond to questions about the impact to the international STEM talent pipeline.

High cost

The OPT programme has expanded dramatically over the past decade, as international students have taken advantage of it to work at top tech companies such as Google and Amazon. Last year the number of recent graduates enrolled rose by 14%, even as the number of new international students dropped, notes Violet Buxton-Walsh, an immigration policy researcher at the Institute for Progress, a non-profit think tank in Washington DC. Despite restrictions on immigrants, “[t]here are very few who have better options than staying in the U.S.,” she says.

Canada recruits dozens of US scholars — including several science stars

The administration’s proposal, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, would require graduates to pay a $70,000 charge for their first year of OPT; STEM graduates would pay an additional $30,000 for a two-year extension.

Without the lure of OPT, the number of international students in the United States is likely to drop sharply, multiple scholars told Nature. As a result, Clemens projects that US colleges and universities could lose a combined $2.5 to 4.2 billion each year in tuition and other revenue.

Ina Ganguli, an economist of science and innovation at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, says the impact goes beyond numbers and finances. “It will change the type of students who are going to come to the US”, she says, because top prospects have the freedom to look elsewhere.

rss_12_1791584812.title: How to build a mouse: embryo development captured in stunning detail
rss_12_1791584812.text:
By introducing and tracking mutations as the cells of a mouse embryo divide, researchers have mapped relationship between cells. Credit: Steve Gschmeissner/Science Photo Library

‘Cell recorders’ based on gene editing have captured mouse development in unprecedented detail.

Two independent teams of scientists published the findings today in Science and in Cell. One team recorded the cell-by-cell development of a two-week-old embryo from a single fertilized egg1, and the other captured most of the cell divisions in embryos as organs formed2.

Both studies were inspired by a landmark early-1980s effort: the first — and still only — full map of animal development. Using only a microscope, UK biologist John Sulston observed each cell of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans as the animal grew from an egg into an adult with precisely 959 somatic, or fully differentiated, cells.

Tracing the lineage of most other animals in this way, particularly mammals, isn’t possible, says Jay Shendure, a genome scientist at the University of Washington in Seattle, who led the Science study. C. elegans is transparent, and each worm develops in precisely the same way, with the same 959 cells having followed an unvarying pattern of cell divisions.

But in mammals such as mice — in which development is hidden and cells number in the billions — external cues such as growth factors influence whether a cell's fate, for instance, whether it will end up in the lungs or liver.

Bizarre CRISPR enzyme kills cancer cells by shredding their DNA

A key question in biology, says Shendure, is how such randomness can give rise to individuals of the same species that have broadly the same form. “Twins look the same, humans kind of look the same, yet even twins develop through very different sets of cell divisions,” he says.

Barcode tracking

Shendure first tackled this question around 2016, when he and his team developed a method based on the gene-editing technology CRISPR that introduced ‘barcodes’ — gene edits at particular locations — into the cells of developing zebrafish (Danio rerio)3. The team then used DNA sequencing to check which barcodes were present in various cells, and inferred relationships between them.

But these CRISPR-based 'lineage recorders' can harm cells if too many edits are introduced during development, says Jonathan Weissman, a molecular biologist at the Whitehead Institute in Cambridge, Massachusetts, who led the study in Cell.

To circumvent these issues, the teams led by Shendure and Weissman used a more precise and less damaging technique, called prime editing, to introduce edits as cells divided during embryo development.

Shendure’s team took a fertilized mouse egg and applied a technique they have named DNA Typewriter, which adds sequential, indelible genetic marks to specific spots in the genome as cells divide. The egg was then implanted into a mouse. After two weeks, when the embryo had formed major organ systems, the researchers read the DNA Typewriter edits and were able to reconstruct the relationships of 1.3 million edited cells —about 10% of the embryo’s total.

rss_13_1791584813.title: Woody ‘blankets’ are being deployed on Arctic permafrost to reduce carbon emissions
rss_13_1791584813.text:
As permafrost thaws in the Arctic, a company wants to use blankets to prevent erosion of the landscape.Credit: Jeff Vanuga/Nature Photo Library/Science Photo Library

A Canadian start-up firm is developing a way to prevent greenhouse-gas emissions from permafrost by stabilizing the soil with an insulating ‘blanket’ of woody materials. If the method works, it could be the first tool to directly forestall green-house gas emissions that are escaping from permafrost as the Arctic heats.

“Our goal is to make sure the carbon in the soil remains buried,” says Cansu Culha, co-founder of PermaC and a natural-hazards researcher at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, Canada.

Earth’s frozen environments are thawing as temperatures rise in response to human emissions. The only reliable way to slow that melting on a global scale is to slash emissions from the burning of fossil fuels. But some researchers are exploring methods to prevent the thaw directly, ranging from placing reflective mats on glaciers to pumping water onto sea ice to thicken it.

Researchers say that PermaC’s approach is the first they know of to focus on preventing permafrost thaw and its associated emissions, which are estimated to be equivalent to those of Japan.

The company just completed the first test of its insulating blankets in Canada’s Northwest Territories at an area of rapidly eroding permafrost known as a retrogressive thaw slump. These slumps occur when a hill of permafrost thaws and collapses, enabling erosion to take big bites out of the landscape. This exposes deeper layers of soil to warming, forming hotspots of CO 2 and methane emissions. One estimate suggests that these areas of rapid erosion could amplify permafrost emissions by as much as 40% compared to models that only account for gradual thaw.

The company’s approach is to stabilize the edge of the slumps with a layer of wood shavings, soil and native seeds, and a burlap-like mat of coconut husks. Culha says she got the idea after hearing about Indigenous communities in Alaska that prevent permafrost degradation by planting trees along the edges of slumps. Similar erosion-control blankets are used in temperate areas, but they haven’t been used to insulate or stabilize permafrost until now, she says.

PermaC has yet to release results from this year'stest. But the blanket seems to have halted erosion: over the Arctic summer, the edge of the slump without the blanket retreated by 5 metres, whereas the blanketed area saw no measurable retreat, Culha says.

“That’s very promising,” says Christina Schaedel, a permafrost scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Falmouth, Massachusetts, who has been advising the company. However, the result is from only one slump over one summer, she adds.

Green blanket

One challenge is calculating how much CO 2 the blankets prevent from being emitted. Measuring the CO 2 emissions from slumps is not straightforward and remains an active research question, says Mark Lara, a biologist who studies permafrost landscapes at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. “There definitely are slumps that are spewing out carbon,” he says. But there are “lots of minutiae that could dramatically impact the results”, he adds. For instance, the emissions from any given slump depend on its geometry, the amount of carbon in the soil and how much of that carbon ends up as CO 2 or methane after erosion.

So far, Culha has only rough estimates for the emissions that the blankets might prevent. Extrapolating from research on erosion rates and soil carbon in the Arctic, she thinks that about 2,200 tonnes of CO 2 a year might be prevented from being emitted at the average carbon-rich slump. If those calculations are accurate and the blankets can be installed at 20,000 slumps across Canada and Alaska — the company’s ambitious goal over the next decade — she estimates that they might prevent about 40 million tonnes of CO 2 emissions a year, roughly equivalent to the annual emissions of Hungary.

Culha says the company is developing a detailed methodology that a third party could use to verify prevented emissions, which would be necessary for the company to sell carbon credits for emissions the blankets prevent. People could purchase those credits to offset emissions elsewhere. The firm aims to issue credits as soon as next year, and has so far raised Can$1.4 million (US$1 million) from investors, says Culha.

rss_14_1791584815.title: Will AI scoop your science? Some researchers see a gloomy future
rss_14_1791584815.text:
As AI agents’ scientific prowess grows, some scientists worry about getting scooped not just by human rivals, but also by bots. Credit: Getty

As AI agents’ ability to do science autonomously continues to improve, scientists are facing a once-unthinkable question: will I get scooped by a bot?

At least twice in the past five weeks, researchers have said that they had been working for an extended period on a particular research question, only to learn that artificial-intelligence companies had either answered the question before them or announced results before they were ready to do the same. In response, researchers who are worried that AI tools might scrape their unpublished work and scoop them are limiting their use of such tools.

Anthropic’s AI biolab finds ‘CRISPR-like’ DNA in viruses. What’s next?

Nevertheless, some AI researchers, although not all, say that AI agents are increasingly likely to reach conclusions before scientists can do so. Researchers are “going to be scooped, but not because they’ve uploaded a manuscript”, says Geoffrey Irving, chief scientist at Resolution, an AI-safety research organization in Berkeley, California. “They’re going to get scooped because the AIs are very good at solving problems, and they’re going to get better and better.”

Controversial findings

On 7 September, Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University in New York City, posted online that he and a collaborator had made progress on the Navier–Stokes problem, a long-standing open question in fluid dynamics. According to Buckmaster’s account, he and Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at the AI company Anthropic, based in San Francisco, California, whose work with Buckmaster was a personal project, had been pursuing the problem for a year. Buckmaster’s 7 September post also included a paper with the solution to a simpler version of the problem. The next day, 8 September, OpenAI, also in San Francisco, announced that its agents had solved the puzzle — a timing that Buckmaster has publicly questioned.

Who gets credit in the AI era? OpenAI maths bombshell sparks debate

Buckmaster raised the possibility that information that he and Alpöge had uploaded to an OpenAI tool could have been used to train the company’s models. OpenAI disputed this scenario. The company said in a statement that an investigation had confirmed that Buckmaster’s “prompts” in the two months before the 8 September announcement “could not have influenced the system in any way, including through training”. The statement also said that OpenAI’s researchers and agents “did not see any of their [Buckmaster and Alpöge’s] work through any means until they released it publicly”.

Two weeks later, Anthropic announced that agents running on its Claude large language model (LLM) had discovered that certain viruses have a pattern of repeated DNA segments similar to the pattern seen in CRISPR gene-editing systems. After the announcement, Mario Rodríguez Mestre, a PhD student in computational biology at the University of Copenhagen, told The New York Times that he has been studying the same DNA patterns for several years, often using Claude, but has not published the work. Mestre also raised the possibility that information his team had uploaded to Anthropic’s tools could have been incorporated into Claude’s training data. Anthropic told the Times that its model was “not trained on any user transcripts”.

Lack of trust

Despite these reassurances, some scientists are now re-evaluating how they use AI. Sandra Laurentino, a reproductive epigeneticist at the University of Münster in Germany, says she no longer trusts AI systems. She now uses AI only to check why her code fails, and before doing so changes all of the parameter and variable names to generic labels such as “group A has feature X” to avoid giving the system information about her experiments. “I am quite careful when it comes to AI,” she says, but the recent controversy has “made me even more paranoid”.

The AI discoveries have also made Samuel Mehr, an auditory cognitive scientist at the University of Auckland in New Zealand, even more hesitant to use commercial AI models than he already was. He has created an AI-use policy for his laboratory that forbids students from uploading protected information to commercial LLMs and warns against using the models for any part of the research process. “I think it’s incredibly risky to hand out your intellectual property to third parties when you don’t know what they’re going to do with it,” he says.

rss_15_1791584816.title: Plague scare: what scientists know — and what Russia won’t say
rss_15_1791584816.text:
The plague bacterium Yersinia pestis (shown here in an electron microscope image) circulates naturally in some parts of the world in wild rodents.Credit: Eye Of Science/Science Photo Library

The death of a 28-year-old researcher at a Siberian laboratory, possibly from pneumonic plague, has triggered international alarm over whether the incident could spark a wider outbreak. Biosecurity specialists have been assuring the public that this is highly unlikely. Their concern about the incident is the lack of transparency around it.

Although news sources have reported that about 200 people at the lab might have been exposed to the researcher and quarantined, Russia’s public-health regulator has insisted that there was “no emergency” at the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Irkutsk, and that the researcher died from pneumonia of “unknown” origin.

Black Death bacterium has become less lethal after genetic tweak

The Russian government’s sparing disclosures combined with unverified rumours of a lab accident have fuelled demands by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the US government for epidemiological data. Only on 7 October — five days after the researcher’s death — did Russian officials reveal that the researcher had been vaccinated against the plague, and that “thousands of tests” revealed that neither she nor others who might have been exposed had tested positive for dangerous pathogens.

Russia has dismissed the concerns over secrecy, with Kremlin officials telling news outlet CNN that it has kept the WHO informed “in accordance with established practice”.

Although the risk of a wider epidemic is minimal — the Yersinia pestis bacterium that causes the disease is treatable with antibiotics — the incident exposes vulnerabilities in global biosurveillance, says Gregory Koblentz, a biosecurity-policy specialist at George Mason University near Washington DC, who studies lab safety.

Nature spoke with Koblentz about why pandemic fears are misplaced and the dangers of government secrecy when responding to this type of incident.

Gregory Koblentz studies laboratory safety at George Mason University near Washington DC.Credit: Rod Lamkey/Abaca Press/Shutterstock

There is a reason the Black Death happened 600 years ago, when we didn’t have sanitation, hygiene or modern medicine. Today, we are much better prepared to handle plague than back then.

Post-COVID-19 pandemic, there is this speculation: “Is this going to be COVID-26?” SARS-CoV-2 was a novel virus for which we didn’t understand the immunology, and didn’t have antivirals or vaccines. In contrast, Y. pestis is a very well-studied, well-characterized bacterium for which we have lots of different antibiotics and for which there are vaccines available.

The WHO [which held a press briefing on 6 October] characterized it well: there is a low risk for people who live in Irkutsk, an even lower risk across Russia, and an extremely low risk for Europe and the world.

Rumours online suggested that the Irkutsk institute is conducting bioweapons research. Is there any evidence for that?

Plague is endemic in that part of the world, so there is a legitimate public-health reason to do research on Y. pestis to develop diagnostic and detection methods at such a lab.

I’m not aware of any historical evidence linking this institute to the Russian bioweapons programme. Russia has at least three known military facilities that do research on biological weapons, so those would be where the programme is mostly located. Conflating this accident with Russian bioweapons research activities is not helpful because this was a public-health lab where this accident happened. The idea that all public-health labs are secretly working on bioweapons is just nonsense.

Separately, Russia inherited the world’s largest bioweapons programme when the Soviet Union fell apart, and for the last 10 years or so, they have been modernizing that programme. That is a major concern, because it’s a violation of the 1972 Biological Weapons Convention [which internationally banned the development, production and stockpiling of biological weapons].
